    Huron · Implementation atlas

    Catalog and its Collaborators

    Stable hierarchy identities meet Raw revisions, Security authority and Foundation values: domain-owned workflows, rules and the adapters that persist them.

    Explicit domain ownershipRules and workflows colocated16 UML viewsOffline-ready

    Implementation snapshot: 16 September 2026, working tree based on e71e685. The editable Markdown source contains all Mermaid diagrams and responsibility notes.

    The catalog gives Huron its stable identities, discoverable hierarchy, immutable Raw revision records, named releases, descriptive metadata, and governance records. Rules and workflows are colocated under domain-owned Core: Catalog owns hierarchy identity and descriptions; Raw owns revisions, uploads and releases; Security owns governance; Foundation owns shared values and pure primitives. Metastore and Rawstore are Core adapters; the API constructs and exposes the public operations.

    This is one class model presented in focused views. It includes every class, protocol, and enum retained from the former catalog model, with their current owners identified below, the related workflows and ports, and their principal persistence adapters. Repeated boxes denote the same class. Neighboring authentication/RBAC classes and application wiring are shown only at their points of collaboration; their internals and the separate operator-only core/integrity maintenance subsystem are outside this atlas. Methods show the public operations and important types, with long parameter lists abbreviated. Private helpers appear where they explain structure. This is a Python class diagram, not a database ER diagram or an exhaustive signature reference.

    Currency matters: the core map describes the same domain-owned working tree. Public operation imports come from each owner's root; links to _impl files identify implementation, not supported cross-package imports. The catalog design and roadmap also describe future work; database tables, enums, protocols, or error names alone do not prove that a workflow is delivered.

    Reading the diagrams

    • A --> B: association/reference, including ID-based domain relationships.
    • A ..> B: uses, creates, or returns B; the label states which.
    • A *-- B: A contains B as part of its object structure.
    • A --|> B: actual Python inheritance.
    • A ..|> B: structural conformance to a Python protocol, not inheritance.
    • <<Protocol>>, <<Frozen>>, <<Enum>>, and <<DeclarationOnly>> identify roles.
    • Multiplicities describe the domain relationship, not preloaded object graphs. Organization/project/dataset links are stored as IDs, not nested child lists.
    • Frozen dataclasses prevent field reassignment; nested lists/dictionaries are not necessarily deeply immutable. Release is write-once through its workflow but its Python dataclass is not frozen.

    1. Catalog and its collaborating owners at a glance

    Owner Values, rules and operations in this atlas
    core.catalog Organization, Project, Dataset, EntityRef, PlatformRoot, Window, DescriptionChange; lifecycle/layer vocabulary, hierarchy and generation paths; CatalogCreation and typed collections.
    core.raw RevisionRef/RevisionRecord, Release, SessionLedger, ExpiryReport, PayloadFile, LedgerEntry, AuditEvent, OutboxEvent; manifest, metadata, documents, ingest transitions, amendments, revision/staging/tag paths; RawRuntime, ingestion, revision reads and Releases.
    core.foundation Slugged and lexical names, identifiers, canonical JSON/record conversion, Clock, IdempotencyClaim, Replay, RetryTransaction and request fingerprints.
    core.security Authenticated Principal and narrower RbacPrincipal, AccessPolicy, governance values/workflows, CatalogFacts and BindingFacts; authentication and role rules.
    core.metastore / core.rawstore Concrete persistence and filesystem adapters; no authority decisions.

    Mixed-file symbols have distinct source locations: DescriptionChange and Window are Catalog values; PayloadFile and SessionLedger are Raw results; IdempotencyClaim, Replay and Clock belong to Foundation. CatalogFacts belongs to Security, GenerationStorage to Catalog, and RevisionStore to Raw.

    The permitted direct domain graph is Security → Foundation; Catalog → Security + Foundation; Raw → Catalog + Security + Foundation + Schema; Integrity → Catalog + Raw + Foundation + Schema. Metastore may use Catalog, Raw, Security and Foundation; Rawstore's only Huron dependency is schema.storage. This is a package DAG, not a claim about every internal module. Migration verification is recorded in the roadmap.

    The overview follows a dataset from identity to published revision and release. CatalogCreation also creates organizations and projects. All seven domain entry classes shown use AccessPolicy; the detailed views below expose those references and the neighboring governance operations.

    Responsibility Owner Important contract
    Create stable identities CatalogCreation Validate slugs/classification/entry layer; authorize parent; claim retry identity; insert record and write generation. Dataset creation creates no revision.
    Discover and edit descriptions Typed collections Current visibility; hidden and absent resources both fail as not found; keyset pagination; immutable slug; version-guarded updates.
    Pin releases core.raw.Releases A tag names one registered revision of that dataset; lookup adds no committed-state or payload-read predicate. Creation is write-once and retry-aware.
    Decide access core.security.AccessPolicy and rules Actor comes from authentication; ancestry comes from server records; bindings are read afresh. Discovery and permission to read bytes are distinct.
    Administer governance Bindings, Policies, ServiceAccounts Each guarded mutation uses the target's scope and authenticated provenance. Policy definitions are opaque stored JSON, not an implemented policy interpreter.
    Produce Raw revisions RawIngestionService / IngestService Every upload submits its complete files; verify actual transfer, freeze commit evidence, publish storage, then record revision/events/receipt.
    Serve revision files RevisionReadService / RevisionService Re-resolve the revision and its current Raw-read permission; select payloads from the committed manifest.
    Persist state and bytes Metastore / rawstore adapters PostgreSQL transactions, visibility predicates, uniqueness and CAS; filesystem generation/tag/envelope operations.

    2. Identity, revisions, releases, and paths

    Sources: Catalog values, Raw values, Catalog lifecycle, Catalog paths, Raw paths, Foundation names.

    Organization, Project, and Dataset are separate concrete classes, not subclasses of an entity base. Their describe() methods share the pure private _describe() function: reject a changed slug, check the expected version even on a no-op, and return either the original object or a successor with both counters advanced. Classification and dataset profile/entry-layer configuration are not descriptive update fields. Creation currently stores profile name/version verbatim. DatasetLifecycle supplies vocabulary; it does not implement retirement or supersession operations.

    Path functions consume Slugged, construct immutable identity-bearing paths, and parse them into RevisionPath. StagingPaths names the separate transfer, completion, and candidate-envelope locations; it does not represent a revision.

    3. Identity creation, discovery, and description services

    Sources: Catalog public exports, creation implementation, collections implementation, generation documents, Raw releases, Catalog retry.

    The collection superclass fixes its reader, entity kind, and parent kind at construction. This is the actual inheritance in the catalog workflow surface; the other operation classes use composition.

    Write ordering: creation and descriptions stage the database change, write canonical generation JSON through GenerationDocuments, then commit the database transaction. Releases similarly insert the release, write its tag document, and record the retry receipt inside the transaction. A storage failure rolls back the database work; a later database rollback does not undo already-durable filesystem writes. These are ordered operations across two stores, not a distributed transaction. claimed_result() handles claim/replay inside the caller's transaction.

    4. Core-owned persistence interfaces

    Sources: Catalog ports, Raw ports, Security facts, Foundation retry.

    These interfaces belong to their consumers: Catalog owns readers/creation/descriptions, Raw owns revision/ingest/release persistence, Security owns CatalogFacts, and Foundation owns retry primitives. HierarchyStore does not include Catalog mutation, Security facts or release writes. A concrete adapter can satisfy all these narrow contracts with one shared transaction writer; application wiring proves conformance. A Catalog Window contains only admitted rows; has_more reflects another visible row, not another hidden row. Hierarchy cursors use (slug, UUID); release cursors use (tag,).

    Claims are scoped by principal and key. Reusing a live key for a different request digest is an error. Replay.kind distinguishes organization, project, dataset, release, ingest-session, in-progress ingest-commit, and committed-revision receipts.

    5. Authorization and governance

    Sources: Security exports, access implementation, scopes, bindings, policies, service accounts, identity, Security values.

    • Bindings requires rbac.binding_manage at the grant's actual scope. Reading and revoking by binding ID resolve that binding before checking its scope.
    • Policy definitions are creatable/listable by any authenticated actor. Attachment requires {scope}.policy_attach; there is no SYSTEM attachment. Storage preserves spec verbatim; this workflow does not enforce retention, quota, or disclosure policy semantics merely because a definition exists.
    • Service-account administration requires service_account.manage on the owning organization. Accounts receive synthesized organization-scoped authority rather than human role grants. ServiceAccounts.disable_service_account() marks the account disabled; IdentityService additionally revokes its credentials.
    • Workflow methods derive created_by and attached_by from their bound actor; callers do not supply those arguments. Persistence ports receive that provenance.

    6. Raw ingestion and revision reads

    Sources: Raw public exports, RawRuntime, ingestion interface, private ingest mechanics, revision interface, private reader, ingest values, result values.

    The domain session owns legal transitions and lease checks; it does no I/O. State transitions return successors and advance the etag; renewal preserves it. The normal path is PREPARING → UPLOADING → VERIFYING → COMMITTING → COMMITTED. COMMITTING can re-enter on a retry or be fenced into RECOVERING; RECOVERING can only finish COMMITTED or FAILED. Abort is restricted to pre-commit states. Each IngestFile proves both part receipt and observed whole-file size/digest. compute_upload_plan() requires every file's complete bytes, including an upload part for an empty file. There is no parent-manifest diff or carry-forward action.

    The actor-bound facade enforces ownership, target discovery, and Raw-write access; abort and ledger reads have specific owner/project-administrator rules. The internal IngestService is not an alternative authorization entry point. Revision discovery alone does not grant download access: manifest/payload reads re-resolve the authoritative revision and require data.read on Raw.

    7. Manifests, metadata, commit evidence, and events

    Sources: Raw manifest, Raw metadata, Raw documents, Raw publication values, Foundation canonical JSON.

    The static marker in the diagram denotes class-level construction methods (@classmethod in Python). validate_manifest() is the validation boundary for manifest entries; their dataclass constructors do not enforce all path/size rules. The document compose()/decode() factories validate schemas and canonical bytes. CommitIntent.__post_init__() additionally checks consistency across all evidence.

    Publication responsibilities:

    1. Freeze the canonical command, manifest, metadata, and COMMITTED marker in a transaction with the COMMITTING transition and reserved retry receipt.
    2. Verify/publish the exact stored envelope through RawStore.
    3. In a short database transaction, insert RevisionRecord, advance the session to COMMITTED, insert AuditEvent and OutboxEvent, and remember the revision receipt. Retried commands must agree with the frozen evidence.
    4. Update RevisionIndex as a best-effort derived navigation aid. INDEX.json does not make a revision authoritative.

    An outbox record is implemented; an operational search projection consumer is not implied by that record. Likewise, audit/outbox subjects here describe Raw publication, not a delivered general-purpose scientific lineage graph.

    8. Layer rules and metadata amendments

    Sources: Catalog layers, Raw amendments.

    These modules deliberately use pure functions, not invented service classes:

    Module Functions and responsibility
    layers.py parse_layer, parse_entry_layer, validate_entry, validate_promotion, required_capability, writable_layers_for_kind, ensure_layer_writable, entry_layers: legal layer vocabulary, direct entry, promotion edges, principal-kind write rules, capability names.
    amendments.py validate_amendment, fold_amendments: allowed-field/reclassification checks and ordered overlay of changes. Pure mechanics exist; an amendment publication workflow is planned.
    raw/manifest.py, foundation/canonical.py Raw owns validate_manifest and validate_manifest_path; Foundation owns canonical_bytes and content_identity.
    catalog/paths.py, raw/paths.py, foundation/names.py and identifiers.py Catalog hierarchy/generation/cross-layer paths; Raw revision/staging/tag paths; Foundation lexical validation and uuid7() identities.
    ingest.py compute_upload_plan, revision_record, revision_committed: pure plan and record/event construction.
    documents.py manifest_bytes, decode_manifest, revision_from_storage: validated persistence round trips and reconstruction.
    foundation/canonical.py, catalog/types.py Foundation owns jsonable and jsonable_value; Catalog owns shared _describe invariants.
    Owned helpers Catalog retry.claimed_result; Foundation request_sha256; Raw session_claim; Security scope resolution.

    Raw, Bronze, and Silver are valid entry configurations; Gold always requires derivation. Declaring a non-Raw entry layer or returning a layer description does not implement its ingestion, array storage, compute, or publication workflow.

    9. Persistence adapters and transaction composition

    Sources: Metastore hierarchy, queries, ingest, RBAC, Security fact projections, Rawstore.

    The production hierarchy adapter owns three fixed typed reader objects; its transaction creates a writer bound to one acquired PostgreSQL connection. That writer inherits ingest persistence and contains three typed CAS description writers. _Projection contains trusted SQL and its decoder; it is not a search index. The memory adapter provides an alternate implementation at the same seams, with staged writes in TransactionBuffer. It does not prove database locks or filesystem durability.

    RawStore is declared in core.raw.ports; Catalog separately consumes core.catalog.ports.GenerationStorage. PosixRawStore satisfies both structurally and imports only schema.storage from Huron. It owns byte I/O, verification, sealing, and durable filesystem publication; it does not decide whether a scientist may publish into a project. Its internal filesystem helpers are implementation details of that neighboring package.

    10. Application construction and lifetime

    Sources: app.py, runtime.py, dependencies.py.

    The application lifespan initializes storage, constructs the adapters and internal operations, publishes ApiRuntime, and closes owned resources. Dependency functions construct actor-bound collections/services using that runtime; the factories are functions, not classes. Domain packages never import ApiRuntime, FastAPI, asyncpg, or PosixRawStore; concrete adapters now live inside Core. The application's capabilities.Storage and capabilities.HierarchyStore compose narrow ports for wiring only. ApiStores is an injection bundle; it is not a catalog repository facade and is not itself a stored field of ApiRuntime.

    11. Planned capabilities, not runtime declarations

    Search projection, scoped credential vending and job dispatch remain planned capabilities. Their unused placeholder ports have been retired from runtime source. Authentication is implemented by Security's credential mechanisms and complete workflows; see the authentication atlas.

    LanceDB search, projection workers, Ray-backed processing, snapshot/product publication, complete lineage traversal, retention execution, and the schema registry workflows remain design/roadmap work. No invented CatalogSearchService, Snapshot, Product, or LineageService class appears here merely because the architecture or database has a corresponding concept.

    12. Shared and owner-specific error hierarchy

    Sources: Foundation errors, Raw errors, Catalog errors, Security errors, API-only errors, Catalog layer errors. All leaves below inherit directly from DomainError. The panels group names for readability; the groups are not additional Python base classes. Some errors reserve contracts for planned operations; their existence does not establish a raise path.

    Foundation owns the common base, retry, precondition, not-found and path failures. Raw owns ingest, manifest, release and amendment failures; Catalog owns identity and reserved projection, layer, snapshot, product, validation and retention vocabulary; Security owns governance, identity, grant and input-access failures. InvalidCursor and DependencyUnavailable belong to the API. This is the retained cross-owner error coverage, not a claim that all leaves belong to Catalog.

    DomainError is framework-free but carries status codes and as_problem() data for the transport contract. Direct instantiation is explicitly refused, rather than enforced through abc.ABC. PathRuleViolation can choose a more specific code per instance. API exception handlers serialize these errors to HTTP problems.

    Source and behavioral cross-checks

    The implementation snapshot was traced through constructors, fields, inheritance, protocol declarations, and wiring. Useful behavioral entry points for our next discussion are:

    • Catalog lifecycle tests and hierarchy record tests: creation, discovery, descriptions, and immutable update rules.
    • Creation integration tests, description integration tests, release integration tests, and catalog store contracts: workflow and adapter behavior.
    • Ingest domain tests, document tests, and core workflow tests: transitions, evidence, actor-bound operations, and retry behavior.

    This document describes inspected implementation; it does not claim that the application test suites were rerun to create a diagram.
